name: Growth hormone peptides at bedtime

card.summary: Using GH-releasing peptides such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295 before sleep to boost the night-time GH pulse; no studies test this practice.
card.note: Unapproved research-peptide use; no studies of the bedtime practice itself.

quick.overview:
Some online users take growth hormone secretagogue peptides, such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295, shortly before bed, on the reasoning that this adds to the natural growth hormone pulse that occurs during sleep.

The peptides are a recognised drug class, mainly studied for growth hormone deficiency. No published study has tested the bedtime practice or appearance outcomes from it.
quick.mechanism: Growth hormone secretagogues act on the ghrelin receptor or on the GHRH receptor to stimulate pituitary growth hormone release, and many also raise IGF-1. Practitioners say bedtime timing aligns the dose with the body's own nocturnal release.
quick.risks: These compounds are not approved for cosmetic use. Many secretagogues also raise prolactin and cortisol. Products sold as research chemicals are unregulated, and no safety data exist for the bedtime practice.

lead: Growth hormone peptides at bedtime is a practice in which people use growth hormone secretagogues, such as ipamorelin, CJC-1295 or sermorelin, shortly before sleep. The goal is to add to the pulse of growth hormone (GH) that the body releases during early deep sleep, with the aim of supporting recovery, leaner body composition and a more youthful look.[1][5]

The appearance chain proponents describe runs through GH and IGF-1: more GH at night means more IGF-1, which is linked to muscle growth, fat breakdown and tissue repair, so training recovers faster and body composition shifts toward more muscle and less fat. Some also expect better skin and sleep quality. In forum discussion the practice is mostly framed around sermorelin and related peptides, and is sometimes paired with advice to get IGF-1 measured by blood test first.[6][7]

Growth hormone secretagogues are a recognised drug class that stimulate GH secretion by acting on the ghrelin receptor (for example ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and ibutamoren) or on the GHRH receptor (for example CJC-1295, sermorelin and tesamorelin).[1] Their main clinical use is treating growth hormone deficiency.[1] No published trial has tested the bedtime practice, or appearance outcomes from it, in people without a deficiency.
infobox: Largest daily GH pulse about an hour after sleep onset [5]
Unapproved for cosmetic or anti-aging use

paras: The practice combines a class of peptides with a timing rationale. Proponents reason that GH secretion is highest during early sleep and that a secretagogue taken beforehand adds to it.[6] This timing rationale comes mainly from community discussion and not from trials of these peptides.

Different community posts describe the practice with different peptides. Sermorelin posts discuss bedtime timing and its use as a monotherapy in younger people with pituitary reserve; other posts describe stacking ipamorelin with CJC-1295.[6][7]

GH is released from the anterior pituitary in pulses controlled mainly by hypothalamic GHRH and somatostatin. The largest predictable peak comes about an hour after sleep onset, nearly half of daily GH release occurs during the deepest non-REM stages, and sleep deprivation generally suppresses release, especially after early adulthood.[5] Adolescents secrete about 700 micrograms per day and healthy adults about 400.[5]

GH is anabolic: it promotes lipolysis, increases protein synthesis and supports bone mineralization. In adults with deficiency, fat mass rises and muscle mass falls, and replacement therapy is associated with reduced fat and increased lean mass.[5] A 2007 meta-analysis of healthy elderly people given GH reported about 2 kg more muscle and 2 kg less fat without a strength gain.[5]

Secretagogues act on two receptors: the ghrelin or growth hormone secretagogue receptor and the GHRH receptor. Many also raise IGF-1 and other pituitary and hypothalamic hormones, including prolactin and cortisol.[1] Wikipedia lists CJC-1295 as a long-acting GHRH analogue for which a 2006 study reported prolonged GH and IGF-1 stimulation in healthy adults, and tesamorelin as a GHRH analogue studied in HIV-associated lipodystrophy.[1]

The International Olympic Committee and the NCAA ban GH, and WADA introduced blood tests that can distinguish natural from recombinant GH around the 2004 Athens Olympics.[5] In the US, a 1990 federal law made distribution of human GH for non-authorized uses a felony, and the DEA in 2015 published a position treating off-label HGH prescription as illegal; Wikipedia notes that GH's efficacy and safety for anti-aging has not been tested in a clinical trial.[5] Secretagogues sold online as research chemicals are not approved for cosmetic use.

No studies found on bedtime use of these peptides for appearance outcomes. Registered trials involving growth hormone address other settings, such as a 16-person early-phase trial of low-dose GH on insulin sensitivity and cortisol production in GH deficiency, a 44-person phase 3 trial of a long-acting GH (MOD-4023) in children with deficiency, and a 98-child phase 3 trial of GH in children born small for gestational age.[2][3][10] One terminated 8-person trial examined gabapentin and hormone release during sleep in older men.[4]
Many secretagogues raise prolactin and cortisol, and GH itself induces insulin resistance and reduces liver glucose uptake.[1][5] No safety data exist for the bedtime practice itself.

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, GH-releasing peptides are discussed as an alternative to injectable GH, with bedtime timing a frequent topic.[6][7]

claims.claim: Taking a GH peptide at bedtime amplifies the natural sleep pulse
claims.believers: Forum posters say sermorelin and related peptides taken before sleep stimulate the pituitary to release more GH when the natural pulse occurs, and describe timing threads about when to inject.[6][7]
claims.experts: GH naturally peaks about an hour after sleep onset in deep sleep.[5] No published trial has tested whether bedtime secretagogue use changes appearance or recovery outcomes.

claims.claim: GH peptides improve recovery and body composition
claims.believers: A T Nation poster suggested that people with low IGF-1 look into sermorelin as a way to boost GH for recovery after injury.[8]
claims.experts: GH replacement in deficient adults is associated with less fat and more lean mass, and a 2007 meta-analysis in healthy elderly found more muscle and less fat without a strength gain.[5] These findings concern GH, not bedtime secretagogue use.

claims.claim: Peptides are a cheaper, gentler route than GH
claims.believers: Posters describe peptides as inexpensive and discuss on-off cycles from online sellers.[9]
claims.experts: Secretagogues are unapproved for cosmetic use, and products sold as research chemicals are unregulated; many raise prolactin and cortisol.[1]

chain: Adds to the natural early-sleep GH pulse and raises IGF-1
Claimed: better recovery, more muscle and less fat
angle.text: People who use GH peptides at night say they time them to coincide with the body's largest daily GH pulse, hoping for improved recovery, body composition and sleep. The effect on appearance is a claim of users; the bedtime practice has not been studied.
